k: Drink water often through the day, even when you are not thirsty. Water is best; avoid sugary and caffeinated drinks. If you have been sweating heavily, or feel weak or dizzy, oral rehydration salts or an isotonic drink help replace the salt you lose in sweat. Keep a filled bottle with you at Arafah, in Mina, at Muzdalifah and on the walk to the Jamarat. If a doctor limits how much you drink (for example for heart or kidney disease), ask them before you travel how to manage in the heat.

A hand-held umbrella: allowed by most scholars (the Hanafis, the Shafi'is, one narration from Imam Ahmad, and some Maliki authorities such as Khalil). When the Prophet ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah, Usamah and Bilal (RA) were with him: one led his camel and the other held up a cloth over his head to shade him from the heat (Muslim {1}). Some jurists disliked or forbade it, but there is no consensus against it.

Men in ihram must not cover the head. The Prophet ﷺ forbade the man in ihram the turban and the hooded cloak (Bukhari {1}), and scholars agree this rules out a cap, hat or ghutra, or a towel or cloth laid on the head. Shade that does not touch the head is different.
Shade in ihram: what men may use
Tents, buildings and trees: allowed by consensus. On the Day of Arafah the Prophet ﷺ rested in a tent pitched for him at Namirah (Muslim {1}).

Umbrella hats held on by a band round the head: better avoided. Most schools forbid tying a band round the head in ihram; Egypt's Dar al-Ifta allows such a hat only when nothing else is available, with a small charity if it is worn for a whole day, and advises a hand-held umbrella instead.
Women cover their heads as usual, and may use an umbrella.

Groups are given set times for the Jamarat: keep to yours. The Ministry of Hajj and Umrah asks pilgrims to follow the official schedules to cut the risk of heat exhaustion and sunstroke. A later time costs you nothing: on the {1}th, {2}th and {3}th the stoning time starts after midday (about {4} pm in Mina in mid-{M1} {5}) and lasts until sunset (about {6} pm), and most scholars allow the night for those who could not stone by day (the Hanbali school: the next day after midday). On the {7}th the Prophet ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah in the forenoon, and on the later days after midday (Muslim {8}). Take water and an umbrella, and get back into the shade straight after.

<1>Signs:</1> body temperature of {1}°C or more; hot, red skin that may be dry or still sweaty; fast heartbeat and fast breathing; confusion, odd behaviour, or seeing and hearing things that are not there; a seizure; collapse or loss of consciousness.

<1>What to do:</1> call {1} first (or {2}, the Saudi Red Crescent). Then cool the person hard while you wait: move them to shade or air conditioning, remove outer clothing, pour or spray cool water over them, especially the head and neck, and fan them; put ice or cold packs on the neck and armpits if you have them. Do not try to make someone drink if they are confused, drowsy or unconscious. If they become unconscious, lay them on their side in the recovery position and check their breathing; start CPR if there is no sign of life.

Cool off with water: ihram allows it

Pouring water over your head is allowed in ihram. Asked how the Prophet ﷺ washed his head in ihram, Abu Ayyub (RA) had water poured over his own head, passed his hands over it from front to back and said, "This is how I saw him do it" (Bukhari {1}). So pour or spray water on your head, face, neck and arms whenever you feel hot. Men: wet the head directly; do not leave a wet towel or cloth resting on it. If you use wipes or soap, choose unscented ones: perfume is not allowed in ihram.

In Makkah the average May high is about {6}°C, and {7}°C has been recorded in May. The Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah lists where heatstroke is common: tawaf at noon, sa'i when it is crowded and hot, Arafah at noon, and Mina, especially the slaughter areas and the Jamarat, because of the long walk and the crowding at the stoning. Plan your days around these places and hours.

Ibn Mas'ud (RA) reached the big jamrah and stood with the House (the Ka'bah) on his left and Mina on his right. He threw seven pebbles and said: "This is how the one to whom Surat al-Baqarah was revealed ﷺ threw" (Bukhari {1}; Muslim {2}). Stand like this if you easily can. In a crowd, follow the Ministry of Hajj's advice and come from the least crowded side. Scholars such as Ibn Baz and Ibn Uthaymeen make it a condition that each pebble lands in the basin. Do not stop for dua after this jamrah.
The {1}th: where to stand at Jamrat al-Aqabah

After the small jamrah, move a little ahead and out of the path. Face the qibla, raise your hands and make a long dua. After the middle jamrah, step aside to the left, out of the path, face the qibla and make dua again. After Jamrat al-Aqabah, do not stop: walk on. Ibn Umar (RA) did this and said: "This is how I saw the Prophet ﷺ do it" (Bukhari {1}; also Bukhari {2}). Today, make your dua where you do not block anyone.

A full Umrah (seven circuits of tawaf and seven laps of sa'i) is a long walk on an empty stomach, and Makkah is warm in {H1} {1} (February to early {M1} {2}): long-term average daytime highs are about {3}°C in February and {4}°C in March. Consider doing your Umrah after iftar, once you have eaten and drunk. The Ministry of Health advises drinking at least {5} cups of water spread between iftar and suhoor, not all at once at suhoor, limiting tea and coffee, and keeping out of the sun in the daytime. If you feel dizzy or confused or cannot stand, drink water at once, ideally an oral rehydration solution, as the Ministry advises: the sick are excused from fasting and make the day up later (Quran {6}). In the last ten nights the prayers run late, so plan to rest after Fajr or in the afternoon.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever gives a fasting person food to break his fast will have the same reward as him, without the fasting person's reward being reduced at all" (Tirmidhi {1}, which al-Tirmidhi called hasan sahih and al-Albani graded sahih).
